Triggers.value: Weapons or objects used as weapons
Beginning to feel detached or unreal

Maladaptive Strategies.value: Talking with others about the event or its aftermath
wear concealing clothing to avoid being noticed

Threat.value: Sudden movements by others put me immediately on guard
I watch other people closely for signs that they might harm me
I frequently look behind me to check if someone is following me

Memory.value: The memory forces its way into my mind when I do not want it to
When I have memories of what happened I sometimes hear things in my head that I heard during the frightening event.
The memory is so extreme it is hard to believe it actually happened to me

Negative Appraisals.value: What happened to me was deeply unfair and nothing has been done about it
If I think about the event, I will not be able to handle it
I feel like an object, not like a person

vignette: Sister Martha, an 80-year-old African woman and long-serving clergy member in her community, has been struggling with intense psychological distress since fleeing her home country as a refugee. The traumatic event she experienced was deeply unfair, leaving her feeling dehumanized and like nothing had been done to address the injustice she faced. Her symptoms began shortly after arriving in the United States, and they have only worsened over time. Sister Martha has come to believe that if she thinks about the event, she will not be able to handle it. This fear of overwhelming emotion has led her to avoid talking with others about what happened, wear concealing clothing to avoid being noticed, and steer clear of seeking medical or psychological help. One day, while riding a bus, an old weapon displayed in a shop window triggered powerful memories that forced their way into her mind when she did not want them to. The memory was so extreme it felt unreal, yet the sound of gunfire she had heard during the traumatic event played vividly in her head. This experience heightened her sense of threat; now, sudden movements by others put her immediately on guard, and she watches other people closely for signs that they might harm her. She frequently looks behind her to check if someone is following her. Sister Martha’s fear of these memories and the associated triggers has led her to avoid public transport altogether. However, this avoidance behavior itself has reinforced her memory of the traumatic event. Each time she avoids a potential trigger, it seems that the memory asserts its presence more strongly. This cycle has left her feeling increasingly isolated and dehumanized. The injustice of what happened to Sister Martha continues to haunt her thoughts. Her fear that she cannot handle thinking about the event leads her to avoid any discussions or medical help related to her trauma. She feels like an object, not a person, which exacerbates her sense of threat and makes her even more vigilant and suspicious of others. In her role as a clergy member, Sister Martha often has to travel for church-related activities. These duties have become increasingly challenging due to the constant reminders she encounters in public spaces. The combination of these triggers and her negative appraisals of the event creates a self-reinforcing cycle that tightens around her daily life. What finally brought Sister Martha to seek help was the realization that her avoidance behaviors were beginning to affect her ability to fulfill her pastoral duties. She is most afraid of losing touch with her community and feeling further dehumanized, but she hopes that with support, she can regain a sense of control over her life and find peace. Sister Martha’s journey towards recovery will require addressing the potent triggers in her environment, understanding her negative appraisals, and gradually facing the memories that continue to haunt her. By doing so, she aims to break the cycle of fear and isolation and reclaim her identity as a valued member of her community.
